claims.text: The starting catalyst consists of uniformly dispersed Pt or Pt-based high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles on a conductive carbon support.
The catalyst surface is static before oxidative–reductive treatment.
Oxidative–reductive potential cycling in O2-saturated electrolyte induces surface restructuring.
Oxidative–reductive cycling forms a transient, metastable oxy-hydride surface phase on the PGM nanoparticles.
Oxidative–reductive cycling produces sub-nanometric rearranged active sites.
The transient oxy-hydride phase modulates the binding energies of ethanol and ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
Optimized intermediate binding improves the adsorption–desorption balance during ethanol oxidation.
The proposed surface restructuring facilitates a concerted 12-electron and 12-proton ethanol-oxidation process.
The dynamic surface phase minimizes catalyst poisoning.
Formation of the transient oxy-hydride phase enhances ethanol-oxidation activity.
Formation of the transient oxy-hydride phase enhances selectivity toward complete ethanol oxidation.
Formation of the transient oxy-hydride phase improves catalyst durability during ethanol oxidation.
A cycling-pretreated catalyst will have a lower ethanol-oxidation onset potential than an inert-treated control.
A cycling-pretreated catalyst will produce a higher ethanol-oxidation current density than an inert-treated control.
A cycling-pretreated catalyst will produce fewer partial-oxidation products than an inert-treated control.
A cycling-pretreated catalyst will retain performance better during extended chronoamperometry than an inert-treated control.
Constant low potential prevents the reversible restructuring needed for the proposed performance advantage.
Excessively high potential causes irreversible oxidation and eliminates the proposed performance advantage.
The mechanism applies only in potential regimes that support reversible surface restructuring.
The untreated baseline retains a less favorable adsorption environment than the cycling-pretreated catalyst.
